lignes.texte: Your degree and job loyalty are worth nothing.
The biggest shift in corporate America is already underway,
one that will dismantle global capitalism.
And it’s all because of one thing… AI.
Right now, boardrooms across the country are replacing high earning white collar workers
with automated code that costs a fraction of a cent to run. Executives are thinking only
of the profit column and ignoring the warning signs right in front of them.
They think they’re automating the workforce… they’re actually decimating the economy.
At some point over the past 3 years, a specific number started circulating through corporate
finance departments. It’s called revenue per employee, and it measures how much
money a company generates for every person it employs. In today’s economic landscape,
that number is drawing the starkest dividing line in the history of American business.
The AI company behind Claude, Anthropic, generates approximately $9 million in revenue per employee.
OpenAI generates $5.6 million dollars per employee.
Meta? $2.5 million.
Anthropic, a company most companies could not name two years ago,
is making more than 4 times the revenue per employee that Google does.
Corporate executives are not philosophers… and they're not exactly ethically inclined.
Dollars are the bottom line. Most of them see these numbers and ask a very simple question:
What would our margins look like if we ran our company the same way?
Some companies didn’t wait to find out.
Meta, Block and Oracle axed thousands of jobs in a matter of months. Every single
one claimed it was for organizational efficiency;
really it was to “embed artificial intelligence across… operations.”
It was a brutal cull.
But no one was as desperate as Microsoft.
They did something unprecedented in their 51-year history. The tech giants resorted to a voluntary
retirement program. Full buyouts were offered to any worker whose age plus years of service
totalled 70 or more. It was a calculated move to get the dead weight out the door.
Microsoft survived recessions, the dot-com crash,
and the entire smartphone era without even considering that move.
It took AI to get there.
None of these companies announced they were explicitly replacing humans
with software. Instead, they buried the truth in corporate speak. Restructuring.
Streamlining. Rightsizing. Offsetting “other investments.” Strategic workforce realignment.
It all means the same thing.
And they’re all following their fiduciary duty to shareholders with the same logic that made them
successful in the first place. The spreadsheet demanded cuts, so that’s what they’ll do.
The vast majority of those tens of thousands of employees had a mortgage payment due on the first
of the month. They had car payments. Credit card balances to pay. They had the kind of
debt that relies on the assumption that their six-figure salary was a permanent condition…
Because for the past 30 years, it was.
But there’s one thing all of these leaders of industry forgot.
What happens to consumer spending when you lay off the consumer?
That’s the blind spot for every boardroom. Executives only care
about slashing expenses today… not who is left to buy the products tomorrow.
In 2024 there was $1.14 trillion dollars in outstanding credit card debt in the United
States. But that debt isn’t just resting among lower-income households scrambling to make ends
meet. The fastest growing delinquency category was consumers earning $150,000
or more. Between January 2023 and December 2024, their delinquency rate surged by 130%.
For three consecutive years, white collar sectors have cut jobs on net while the
rest of the economy technically grew. In February 2026 alone, 92,000 white-collar
positions were eliminated. In all of 2025, companies announced 1.1 million layoffs,
the highest total since the height of the pandemic, when the entire world had shut down.
This wasn’t caused by a run-of-the-mill recession.
GDP was growing and the stock market, broadly speaking, was fine,
What isn’t fine are the empty desks left behind.
The AI that replaced them doesn’t have a mortgage
or car payments due on the first of the month. It doesn’t buy anything.
It only produces.
It doesn’t consume, in the traditional sense. Or
in the capitalistic sense. And that’s a fatal problem. Because the version
of capitalism America has run for 80 years is powered by consumer spending.
About two-thirds of U.S. GDP comes from people buying things. These people historically got
their money from jobs. Specifically, high-income jobs, because high-income
earners carry a disproportionate share of the debt load the banking system is built on top of.
When you eliminate the six-figure worker,
you do 2 things. You might improve your balance sheet over the short term…
But you also eliminate tens, if not hundreds of thousands of people making the mortgage payment
that services your bank's loan. You eliminate the car payment backstopping the auto lender.
You eliminate the monthly minimum keeping a consumer credit portfolio looking healthy.
All that’s left in these companies are empty desks.
Across major U.S. markets, office vacancy currently sits between about 18 and 22%.
In San Francisco, historically the most expensive commercial real estate market in the country,
vacancy peaked at 36.7%. It has since “improved” to about 30%.
The real estate collapse is just window dressing.
The real impact is in the banking system.
The firms that financed those empty office towers sitting aren’t the ones you’d expect,
like JPMorgan Chase or Citigroup. The banks holding catastrophic
exposure are the small regional banks and community lenders. For these institutions,
commercial real estate loan portfolios represent anywhere from 25 to 40% of their total loan book.
An office tower in St. Louis was recently appraised at 52 cents on the original loan dollar.
The bank that financed it didn’t make a grand announcement. Instead,
they made an internal adjustment to what accountants call the market-to-market
value. It’s a classic delaying tactic to help pretend everything is ok.
This is the same playbook that signaled every banking crash in history.
When office buildings lose value, loans secured against them go underwater. The debt
owed on is more than what the asset is now worth.
When loans go underwater at scale, the regional banks holding them face a balance sheet crisis.
To protect themselves, the banks stop approving loans. That means small
businesses lose access to capital, which results in hiring freezes.
Hiring freezes are the last thing America needs. Especially when the
country is already shedding 92,000 white-collar jobs.
The commercial real estate collapse and consumer debt cascade aren't separate issues.
They’re two fuses burning toward the same explosive.
In May 2026, AI was cited as the reason for 40% of all U.S. layoffs,
the highest monthly proportion ever recorded.
In March and April of the same year, it was already the single
most common justification for workforce reductions. Since tracking began in 2023,
almost 176,000 jobs have been attributed to AI-driven cuts. The unemployment rate in the
country now sits at 4.4%, the highest since the early pandemic recovery.
Workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations
have seen a 16% percent employment decline. Software developers in that same age bracket
are down 20% since late 2022. Big Tech new-graduate hiring d had halved by 2025.
The entryway into the white-collar professional class has started to cave in.
And it triggers a vicious, downward spiral.
When AI replaces the worker, you lose the person keeping the housing market,
retail sector, and banking industry alive.
Corporate America is starving the very system that feeds it.
PwC’s 2026 AI Jobs Barometer found that companies most exposed to AI
are actually growing headcount faster than their less-exposed competitors.
They’re also paying wages that are, on average, 42% higher.
On its face, it looks like a counterargument.
It isn't.
The workers thriving inside AI-exposed companies are just the ones who narrowly
survived the first cut. The ones who were replaced are not included in that survey.
They’re not counted in the wage premium, or reflected in the headcount growth.
Goldman Sachs estimates that between 6 and 7% of the U.S. workforce could be displaced under
widespread AI adoption. McKinsey puts the share of U.S. work hours automatable by 2030 at up to 30%.
But while the middle class is being engineered out of existence,
the architects behind it all are moving their own money.
They’re hiding their money in a shadowy finance sector that most people haven’t heard of.
Family offices.
These aren’t small family owned businesses. They’re private,
elite wealth-management firms built for the sole purpose of
protecting generational money. They have no public shareholders to report
to and zero obligation to tell anyone what they’re doing with the capital they manage.
65% of family offices now prioritize AI investments, up from under 30% in
2023. Among single-family offices managing more than $1 billion, that figure is closer to 80%.
Buying stock in an AI company is gambling that one company wins. This is not what these family
offices are doing. They’re investing in the infrastructure. The data centers. Power grid
capacity. Nuclear energy deals that are structured specifically to serve AI compute clusters.
45% of family office AI deployment goes into foundation models and physical infrastructure.
It is the difference between betting on a horse and buying the racetrack.
Jeff Bezos’ family office alone has committed $12 billion to AI infrastructure. ICONIQ Capital,
which manages $80 billion in assets on behalf of tech billionaires,
co-led Anthropic’s $13 billion dollar funding round.
When the people who built the game start buying the board it’s played on,
you need to pay attention.
In September 2026, Anthropic published an economic research report modeling 3
scenarios for the U.S. economy by 2030. In their most extreme scenario, the one where
AI performs roughly 30% of all cognitive tasks, U.S. GDP grows 32.4% above baseline.
That would have the U.S. economy doubling every 4 and a half years.
But at the exact same time,
white collar employment hits 17.9%. Overall unemployment reaches 11.9%.
How can an economy grow at record speed while millions of office workers lose their jobs?
It’s because of the fundamental shift in who gets paid.
For most of modern history, every dollar the American economy produces gets split two ways:
workers took home about 60 cents. Owners took the other 40.
In Anthropic's scenario,
that flips. Workers take home 45 cents. Owners take the rest… and then some.
The economic pie gets bigger. Workers just get a smaller slice.
That’s exactly why family offices are aggressively buying up AI infrastructure. They
aren’t trying to save the middle class. They’re positioning themselves to reap the rewards.
It’s like selling your soul to the devil. Except
the family offices are the ones holding the contract.
It’s never a great sign in any industry when the people who
built the product start telling you how dangerous it actually is.
But that’s what’s happening in the tech world right now.
Engineers and execs are sounding the alarm as they file their resignation letters.
Mo Gawdat built artificial intelligence inside Google X as Chief Business Officer. He was one of
the architects of the machine. On his departure, he went on a podcast and said the next 15 years
would be, in his exact words, “hell before we get to heaven.” He believed that entry-level
white-collar work would face severe displacement, with 30% of roles in certain sectors gone by 2028.
He also noted that CEO’s weren’t safe either.
Geoffrey Hinton is on a different level to most tech startup CEOs. He’s the reason the
AI industry exists in the first place. The so-called grandfather of AI spent a decade at
Google before quitting in 2023 specifically so he could say the quiet parts out loud.
AI, he claimed, will create "massive" unemployment, accelerate inequality,
and erode human dignity and purpose.
In 2026, he updated his warning to add that the new wave is already arriving and governments
are nowhere near ready for it. Perhaps more shockingly, he claimed humanity was at a turning
point and there was a 10-20% chance AI could decide it doesn’t need us at all and wipe us out.
That’s just his gut feeling.
There’s a pattern emerging from inside OpenAI and Anthropic themselves. Researchers are quitting and
calling for slowdowns. They’re flagging risks that don’t fit into press releases about AGI benefits.
“The world is in peril,” is the standard refrain coming from many people closest to the technology.
Anthropic’s Jacob Coxon claimed that “aI labs are racing toward systems that could kill
everyone.” He added that many of his colleagues “earnestly believe it could kill us all” by 2030.
The race for superintelligence, he believes, is gambling with all of our lives.
As late as 2025, Sam Altman was predicting an AI jobs apocalypse. Then OpenAI’s IPO
timing came into focus, and suddenly the warnings got walked back considerably.
Disruption is a compelling story. Disruption that
collapses consumer demand is a harder prospectus to file.
One of the largest hedge funds on the planet, the Man Group, published a note in 2026 entitled,
“When the AI Bubble Bursts, Don’t Count on the U.S. Consumer.”
Notes like these aren’t meant to be informative. The Man Group manages $175 billion in assets. When
a firm of that size tells its clients not to count on the American consumer, they’ve already moved
the money in anticipation. Their decision will be backed by a spreadsheet that very few will see.
The collapse of the demand engine is already
accounted for by them. And they’re not the only ones.
Goldman Sachs is warning that AI-fueled layoffs could raise the unemployment rate by the end of
2026. And white-collar workers who still have jobs are taking pay cuts just to stay employed.
It’s a sign of a labor market that has
already shifted leverage away from the worker, permanently.
300 million jobs globally, says Goldman. Half of all white-collar entry-level positions,
say the experts. 15 years of hell, says the man who built the machine.
Nobody knows how it ends. But the hedge funds are hedging, the researchers are resigning,
and the corporate elite are moving their wealth off the grid.
They aren’t worrying about the death of the middle class.
They’ve already accepted a world without them.
AI is advancing faster than anyone expected. And that’s got industry
experts sounding the alarm. Watch “Why the AI Safety Teams Are Gone” to find
out how close humanity is to losing the AI revolution. Or click on this.
